pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 1: Introduction to Programming

Every app, game and website was created by people who wrote instructions for computers. Those instructions are called programs. In this unit you will learn the language programmers use, the kinds of data computers work with, and how programs store data in variables and constants.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.4.1.1** Show an understanding of the concept of programming.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.4.1.1.1** Demonstrate the correct use of programming terminologies.
- **B7.4.1.1.2** Demonstrate understanding in the use of data types (e.g. float, integer, string, char).
- **B7.4.1.1.3** Demonstrate the use of constants and variables used in programming.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 11.1 Programming Terminologies
- 11.2 Data Types
- 11.3 Constants and Variables

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1, CC8.2), Digital Literacy (DL5.5, DL6.5), Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (CP5.1).

pages.title: Programming Terminologies
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.4.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- list programming terms in alphabetical order;
- explain each term correctly.
**Programming** (or **coding**) is the process of writing instructions that a computer can follow to solve a problem or perform a task. The people who do it are called **programmers** or **software developers**. Like every profession, programming has its own vocabulary. The table lists the key terms **in alphabetical order** to help you remember them.

pages.title: Programming Terminologies (continued)
pages.body:
| **Term** | **Meaning** |
|---|---|
| Algorithm | A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem |
| Bug | An error in a program that makes it behave wrongly |
| Code (source code) | Instructions written in a programming language |
| Compiler | A program that translates the whole source code into machine code before the program runs (e.g. C, C++) |
| Constant | A named value that does **not** change while the program runs (e.g. PI = 3.142) |
| Data type | The kind of data a value is (integer, float, string, char, Boolean) |
| Debugging | Finding and fixing bugs |
| Event | Something that happens and triggers code to run (e.g. a mouse click, pressing the green flag in Scratch) |
| Execute (run) | To carry out the instructions of a program |
| Flowchart | A diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using standard symbols |
| IDE (Integrated Development Environment) | Software with tools for writing, running and debugging code (e.g. IDLE, Thonny, Visual Studio Code) |
| Input | Data given to a program (e.g. typed by the user) |
| Interpreter | A program that translates and runs code one line at a time (e.g. Python) |
| Iteration (loop) | Repeating a set of instructions |
| Machine code | Binary instructions (0s and 1s) the CPU understands directly |
| Operator | A symbol that performs an operation, e.g. +, −, ∗, /, >, == |
| Output | Information produced by a program (e.g. displayed on screen) |
| Program | A complete set of instructions that a computer carries out |
| Programming language | A formal language for writing programs: Python, Scratch, Java, C++, JavaScript |
| Pseudocode | An algorithm written in structured plain English that looks like code |
| Selection | Choosing between different paths using a condition (IF … THEN … ELSE) |
| Sequence | Instructions carried out one after another in order |
| Syntax | The grammar rules of a programming language |
| Syntax error | A mistake in the rules of the language (e.g. a missing bracket) |
| Variable | A named storage location whose value **can** change while the program runs |

pages.title: Programming Terminologies (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity — Terminology recall game**
Write each term on a card and its meaning on another card. In groups, shuffle the cards and race to match terms with meanings. Then group the terms under headings: **Translating code** (compiler, interpreter, machine code), **Errors** (bug, debugging, syntax error), **Data** (variable, constant, data type), **Control** (sequence, selection, iteration).

pages.title: Data Types
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.4.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain the common data types;
- identify the data type of everyday data.
A **data type** tells the computer what kind of value is being stored and what operations can be carried out on it. For example, you can multiply two numbers, but you cannot multiply two names.
| **Data type** | **Description** | **Examples** | **In Python** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integer (int) | Whole numbers, positive, negative or zero, with no decimal point | 15, −3, 0, 2026 | age = 13 |
| Float / Real | Numbers with a decimal point (fractional part) | 3.142, 1.75, −0.5, 99.9 | height = 1.62 |
| String (str) | A sequence of characters (text) enclosed in quotation marks | "Kofi", "B7 Gold", "0244123456" | name = "Akua" |
| Character (char) | A single letter, digit or symbol | 'A', '7', '?' | Python stores this as a one-letter string: grade = "A" |
| Boolean (bool) | Only two possible values: True or False | True, False | passed = True |
> 🎯 **BECE focus** A phone number such as **0244123456** should be stored as a **string**, not an integer: we never do arithmetic on phone numbers, and an integer would drop the leading zero.

pages.title: Constants and Variables
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.4.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain constants and variables;
- show how they are used in programs;
- discuss the benefits of using variables instead of constants.
Programs store data in memory. A **variable** is like a labelled box whose contents can be changed; a **constant** is like a label engraved on a box whose contents never change.
|  | **Variable** | **Constant** |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | A named memory location whose value can change during the program | A named value that stays the same throughout the program |
| Examples | score, total, name, temperature | PI = 3.142, VAT_RATE = 0.15, DAYS_IN_WEEK = 7 |
| Naming style (Python) | lowercase words, e.g. total_score | UPPERCASE by convention, e.g. MAX_MARK |
## Constants and variables in a program
This short Python program calculates the area of a circle. PI is a constant; radius and area are variables. The # symbol starts a comment that the computer ignores.
> ✏️ **Worked example — Python**
PI = 3.142 # constant
radius = float(input("Enter the radius: ")) # variable from input
area = PI ∗ radius ∗ radius # variable calculated
print("The area is", area)
If the user enters **7**, the program prints: The area is 153.958. Run it again with **10** and it prints 314.2: the **variables** change; the **constant** does not.

pages.title: Constants and Variables (continued)
pages.body:
In **Scratch**, variables are created in the **Variables** category: click **Make a Variable**, name it (e.g. score), then use the blocks set score to 0 and change score by 1. A score in a game is a perfect example of a variable.
## Rules for naming variables
- Use meaningful names: total_marks is better than x.
- Start with a letter or underscore, not a digit (1score is invalid).
- No spaces: use underscores (first_name) or camelCase (firstName).
- Do not use reserved keywords of the language (e.g. print, if, for in Python).
- Names are case-sensitive in most languages: Score and score are different.
## Benefits of using variables instead of typed-in constant values
- **Flexibility:** the same program works for different inputs (any radius, any score).
- **Easy updating:** change a value in one place instead of in every line where it is used.
- **Readability:** price ∗ quantity is clearer than 25 ∗ 4.
- **Storing results** of calculations for later use.
- **Fewer errors:** you don’t have to retype the same number many times.
> 💻 **Practical session — Try it**
Using Scratch or Python (e.g. on trinket.io or Thonny), create a program that stores your name, age and height in variables and displays a sentence such as “My name is Ama. I am 12 years old and 1.5 m tall.” Then change the values and run it again.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Explain the following terms: syntax, debugging, IDE, iteration.
2. Give **one** example of each data type: integer, float, string, char, Boolean.
3. Explain why a phone number should be stored as a string.
4. Distinguish between a variable and a constant, giving examples.
5. State **three** benefits of using variables.
